result:
**Opening argument for c = √2/2 ≈ 0.707**

The lower bound is a concrete construction, and it can be checked directly. Take $S_2 \subseteq V_2$ and $S_3 \subseteq V_3$ with $|S_2| = |S_3| = (n-1)/2$, and include a transversal edge $\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}$ exactly when $v_2 \in S_2$ or $v_3 \in S_3$. Every edge meets $S = S_2 \cup S_3$, and $|S| = n-1 < n$, so $H$ has no perfect matching. For $v_2 \in V_2 \setminus S_2$, the link is $V_1 \times S_3 \cong K_{n,n/2}$, whose spectral radius is $\sqrt{n \cdot n/2} = n/\sqrt{2}$. The other link types are larger: $K_{n,n}$ for vertices in $S$, and about $0.809n$ for $V_1$. So every link has spectral radius at least $(1/\sqrt{2} - o(1))n$ and $H$ has no perfect matching. Hence $c \ge 1/\sqrt{2}$.

For the matching direction, the threshold $n^2/2$ is the minimum degree needed for a bipartite graph with parts of size $n$ to have a perfect matching. The class-blind analysis shows that when every link is complete bipartite, the spectral condition reduces exactly to this degree condition, giving $\sqrt{n \cdot n/2} = n/\sqrt{2}$. Space barriers with more than one class in play produce only rank-2 links with smaller spectral radius, such as $2n/3$. So $n/\sqrt{2}$ is the best possible threshold, and $c = \sqrt{2}/2$.
